681.quote_or_event: “Recognize the Lord's Light within all, and do not consider social class or status; there are no classes or castes in the world hereafter.”
681.explanation: Guru Nanak rejects birth and social rank as a measure of worth, telling the listener to see the one divine Light in every person.
681.tie_back: The Kural counts birth in a family of good standing among an envoy's qualifications; Sikh teaching agrees that a loving nature and refined conduct matter, but explicitly refuses to rank anyone by birth.
681.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 349, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
681._accuracy_note: Mainly a contrast: Sikhism's rejection of caste and lineage conflicts with the Kural's 'good family' criterion, so this marks a real difference rather than a parallel.

682.quote_or_event: Bhai Lehna, who became Guru Angad, is remembered above all for his loyalty to Guru Nanak; having understood his master's ideals, he gave them definite form and, as Guru, standardised the Gurmukhi script in which much of the scripture is written.
682.explanation: Guru Angad's devotion to Guru Nanak, joined to an understanding of what his master intended and a gift for setting it down in words and script, made him Guru Nanak's chosen successor.
682.tie_back: The Kural names love for one's master, knowledge of what serves him, and skill with words as the envoy's three essentials; Guru Angad's loyalty, understanding and work on the written word together show all three.
682._accuracy_note: Partial: the three qualities line up, but Guru Angad was a disciple and successor, not an envoy, and Britannica itself notes that some institutions credited to him rest on tradition rather than documents.

683.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
683.explanation: Guru Nanak says that learning becomes real only when it is reflected on and turned to use for others, not when it is merely possessed.
683.tie_back: The Kural says an envoy among learned ministers and armed kings must be more than learned: he must be able to apply what he knows; Guru Nanak likewise values learning only when it is digested and put to work.
683.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
683._accuracy_note: Next-best only: shares the point that applied learning beats mere learning, but has nothing on diplomacy or on speaking before hostile kings.

684.quote_or_event: “Wisdom leads us to serve our Lord and Master; through wisdom, honor is obtained.”
684.explanation: In Sarang ki Vaar Guru Nanak praises good sense (akal) as what makes one's service to the Master effective and wins honour.
684.tie_back: The Kural wants an envoy with natural good sense, presence and tested learning so that he is respected and succeeds; Guru Nanak likewise links sound judgement to good service and the honour it earns.
684.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
684._accuracy_note: Partial: matches the first quality and the honour it brings, but Gurbani gives no weight to impressive appearance, and the service meant is to God.

685.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all.”
685.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are in the Guru Granth Sahib, forbids even one harsh word on the ground that the Lord dwells in every listener.
685.tie_back: The Kural's true envoy drops harsh words and speaks so pleasantly that listeners agree; Farid's rule against any harsh word gives that diplomatic courtesy a spiritual basis.
685.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
685._accuracy_note: Strong fit on avoiding harsh speech, though Farid's reason is reverence for God in all, not securing advantage for one's king, and he says nothing about brevity.

686.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else - says Nanak, listen, mind: call him spiritually wise.”
686.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur makes fearlessness, together with not intimidating others, a mark of true wisdom; he himself went to his death in Delhi in 1675 rather than yield.
686.tie_back: The Kural's envoy does not flinch at angry looks and knows what the moment needs; Guru Tegh Bahadur's ideal is exactly such composed fearlessness grounded in wisdom.
686.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Salok Mahalla 9 (Salok 16), Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
686._accuracy_note: Strong fit on fearlessness joined to wisdom, though the salok describes the enlightened person generally, not an envoy facing a foreign court.

687.quote_or_event: “Those words are acceptable, which, when spoken, bring honor. Harsh words bring only grief. Listen, O foolish and ignorant mind!”
687.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that speech must be weighed by its effect, since honourable words are accepted and careless or harsh words bring ruin.
687.tie_back: The Kural's foremost envoy rehearses his words, the other side's replies and his own answers before speaking; Guru Nanak likewise asks that words be judged by what they will bring before they are said.
687.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
687._accuracy_note: Next-best only: covers weighing one's words but not the Kural's attention to protocol, the receptive moment or the right place.

688.quote_or_event: After the battle of Chamkaur (1704), Guru Gobind Singh would not trust Mughal couriers with his Zafarnama, a letter rebuking Aurangzeb for breaking his oath of safe passage, so he sent his own Sikhs, Bhai Daya Singh and Bhai Dharam Singh, to carry it to the emperor personally.
688.explanation: The Guru chose envoys whose loyalty and courage he could rely on to deliver a bold, unwelcome message exactly as written, into the hands of a hostile emperor.
688.tie_back: The Kural's envoy who carries his master's message unchanged must be incorruptible, bold and truthful; Daya Singh and Dharam Singh were chosen precisely because they could be trusted to deliver the Guru's words intact.
688.source: Wikipedia, Zafarnama (letter), citing Isher Singh Nara and Louis E. Fenech
688._accuracy_note: Strong fit with a real Sikh envoy carrying a fixed message, but sourced from Wikipedia as a last resort, and details of the delivery (dates, number of Sikhs) are partly uncited there.

689.quote_or_event: Summoned by Aurangzeb, Guru Har Rai sent his son Ram Rai to represent him; when the emperor objected to a line of the Adi Granth as disparaging to Muslims, Ram Rai tried to appease him by claiming it had been wrongly transcribed, and Guru Har Rai excommunicated him for it and passed him over for the succession.
689.explanation: Sikh history remembers Ram Rai as the envoy who, under pressure at a foreign court, let slip words that lowered his own Guru's scripture, and was cast off for it.
689.tie_back: The Kural says only one firm enough never to let a shameful word slip out under pressure is fit to carry his master's message to other kings; Ram Rai is the exact counter-example, and the Guru's response shows how seriously the fault was judged.
689._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: a historical envoy at a hostile court who demeaned his master's word out of fear, though it is a negative example rather than a model.

690.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
690.explanation: Guru Nanak makes readiness to give one's life the condition for entering the path of devotion, a line later embodied in the Sikh martyr tradition.
690.tie_back: The Kural's true envoy delivers his king's message in full even if it costs him his life; Guru Nanak asks the same readiness to lay down one's head for one's Master.
690.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
690._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on loyalty unto death, though Guru Nanak's 'game of love' concerns devotion to God, not service to a human king.
